screens.title: RPM vs DNF — When to use each
screens.narratorSegment: Start by clarifying a common confusion: DNF and RPM are not competing package formats; they occupy different levels of the toolchain. RPM defines the package format and provides commands to operate on single. rpm files and the local RPM database. DNF is a higher-level package manager that uses repositories and resolves dependencies for you. Use rpm when you need precise, local control: installing a single downloaded file, querying exactly which files belong to a package, or verifying file integrity against the RPM database. Use DNF for day-to-day updates, installs from repositories, and when dependency resolution is essential. A useful mental model is that DNF manages collections and relationships, while rpm manages individual package artifacts. Common misconception: rpm will not magically fetch dependencies. If you try to install a. rpm that requires other packages, rpm will fail and report missing dependencies. Conversely, DNF will consult configured repositories and try to install required packages automatically. In practice, system administrators often use rpm for offline installs, forensic verification, or surgical fixes when DNF's higher-level behavior is not desired. As you practice, reflect on a scenario where a local vendor supplies a single. rpm for a custom tool — which tool do you pick and why?

keyIdea.title: Distinction
keyIdea.text: DNF = repository-aware dependency resolver for general use. RPM = low-level tool for single-file control, offline installs, and verification.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › RPM vs DNF
RPM
Low-level manager operating on single .rpm files and the on-disk RPM database. No automatic dependency resolution; used for local installs, verification, and precise queries.
Use when: installing a vendor-supplied .rpm, auditing file integrity, troubleshooting DNF failures.
Command examples: rpm -ivh, rpm -Uvh, rpm -qa, rpm -V, rpm -e
DNF
High-level package manager that resolves dependencies from configured repositories, manages groups, and performs system-wide updates. Preferred for routine installs and updates.
Use when: installing from repos, resolving dependencies automatically, handling updates for many packages.
Command examples: dnf install, dnf update, dnf remove, dnf download
Misconception
RPM will resolve dependencies automatically. It will not; you must handle dependencies yourself.
Pro tip
Use dnf download to obtain a local .rpm from a repo when you need a file for offline install with rpm.
Check your understanding
If a custom vendor provides a single .rpm and you have no repo access, which tool lets you install it directly? (Think of dependency implications.)

screens.title: The RPM database
screens.narratorSegment: The RPM database is the local record the rpm utility uses to track installed packages, their metadata, and the files they installed. On RHEL systems this database is typically stored under /var/lib/rpm. It contains details such as package name, version, release, installed file list, ownership, permissions, and checksums that rpm -V uses for verification. Think of the database as the authoritative ledger that lets you ask: which package owns /usr/bin/tree? Or what version of httpd is installed? When you run rpm -qa you query that ledger to list installed packages. When you run rpm -ql package_name you ask which files that package deposited. Importantly, the database is how rpm can detect unauthorized changes: rpm -V compares the current file state against the stored metadata. A common misconception is that the database contains copies of files; it does not — it contains metadata and hashes. If the database becomes corrupted, rpm commands will fail to report accurate package state, so backups or careful recovery procedures are necessary on production servers. Understanding what the database holds helps you interpret query outputs and verification flags during audits and troubleshooting.

keyIdea.title: Database role
keyIdea.text: The RPM database stores package metadata and file attributes used for queries and verification; it's an authoritative registry, not a copy of installed files.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › RPM Database
What the RPM database stores
  • Package metadata: name, version, release, vendor, build date.
  • File lists: full paths of files installed by each package.
  • Attributes and checksums used by rpm -V (sizes, MD5 sums, permissions, types, owners).
  • Ownership relationships used by rpm -e to check reverse dependencies.
Key question: Which package owns a path? Use rpm -qf /path/to/file to ask the database.
Common queries
rpm -qa
rpm -qi httpd
rpm -ql tree
rpm -qf /usr/bin/tree
Remember: the database stores metadata only. If metadata and actual files differ, rpm -V will flag the discrepancy.

screens.title: Install a local RPM with rpm -ivh
screens.narratorSegment: Installing a local. rpm file with rpm -ivh is a direct, single-file operation. The -i flag requests an install, -v enables verbose output so you see progress, and -h prints hash marks as a simple progress indicator. When you run sudo rpm -ivh /path/to/package. rpm, rpm unpacks the package scripts and files, records metadata in the RPM database, and places the files on disk. However, rpm does not fetch or install missing dependencies; if the package requires libraries or other packages that are not present, rpm will stop and report missing dependencies. That output is your clue: it tells you exactly which packages are required. To resolve those dependencies you can either install the missing RPMs manually, use dnf to fetch them, or use dnf download to obtain RPM files for offline installation. A typical misconception is that adding -U is necessary for installing any new version; -ivh is specifically an install, while -Uvh can both install and upgrade. When a package conflicts with an existing one, rpm will return an error explaining the conflict. In practice, test local installs inside a container or VM so you can safely see dependency failures and learn how to retrieve and satisfy prerequisites.

keyIdea.title: Install pattern
keyIdea.text: Use rpm -ivh for direct local installs but expect to manually resolve dependencies because rpm does not fetch missing packages.

content.html:
Process
Install a local RPM
Follow these steps to attempt a local install and interpret output.
  1. Place the .rpm in a known path, e.g., /tmp.
  2. Run: sudo rpm -ivh /tmp/package.rpm and watch the verbose output and hash marks.
  3. If rpm reports missing dependencies, note the package names it requests.
  4. Either obtain those RPMs and install them, or use dnf to fetch and resolve dependencies.
Misconception: rpm will resolve dependencies. It will not. You must supply or fetch missing packages.
Command example
sudo rpm -ivh /tmp/my_custom_app-1.0-1.el8.x86_64.rpm
If dependencies are missing you'll see output naming the missing packages. Use that list to fetch or install prerequisites.
Scenario card: You have no internet access. Obtain RPMs beforehand or use dnf download on a machine with network access.

screens.title: Upgrade packages with rpm -Uvh
screens.narratorSegment: Upgrading a package with rpm uses the -U flag: rpm -Uvh /path/to/package. rpm. This command installs the new package and removes the old one in the same operation if an earlier version exists. If no prior version is present, -Uvh will simply install the package. The verbose and hash options behave the same as with install. Important: rpm will not automatically resolve any new dependencies introduced by the upgraded version; if the upgrade requires additional packages that are missing, rpm will fail and report the missing items. For routine system updates and dependency-aware upgrades, prefer dnf update because it will consult repositories and try to satisfy requirements automatically. However, rpm -Uvh is useful when you must apply a vendor-supplied update from an offline medium or when you want deterministic control over the exact RPM file being installed. A misconception to avoid is that -Uvh will prevent conflicts: if the new package conflicts with others or introduces incompatible changes, rpm will fail and provide an error. As a best practice, test upgrades in a staging environment or use dnf when networked repositories can provide resolving assistance.

keyIdea.title: Upgrade behavior
keyIdea.text: rpm -Uvh replaces older versions or installs if absent, but it won't resolve new dependencies — use dnf for dependency-aware upgrades when possible.

content.html:
Upgrade
Using rpm -Uvh
Upgrade replaces the previous package if present, or installs if absent. It does not fetch dependencies.
sudo rpm -Uvh /root/my_app-2.0-1.el8.x86_64.rpm
If the new version introduces dependencies, rpm will report them and fail. Use dnf update when you have repository access and want automatic resolution.
Scenario
A vendor sends you an updated RPM to patch a bug. You can use rpm -Uvh to apply that exact file on the server without pulling from a repository. This gives a deterministic, single-file upgrade path.
Common mistake: using -i to 'upgrade' an installed package. -i will attempt to install a new package alongside or conflict — prefer -U for upgrades.

screens.title: Querying the RPM database
screens.narratorSegment: Querying the RPM database is the heart of understanding what is installed and where its files reside. The simplest command is rpm -qa, which lists all installed RPM packages by name. Because the output can be long, you often pipe it to grep to find a package of interest, for example rpm -qa | grep httpd. To see package metadata such as version, vendor, build date, and description, use rpm -qi package_name. To list all files installed by a package, use rpm -ql package_name. This last command helps when you need to locate configuration files or binaries a package provides. Another useful query is rpm -qf /path/to/file which tells you which package owns a specific file on disk. A common mistake is confusing package names used by rpm with the filenames of RPM archives; rpm commands use package names for queries (not the. rpm filename). Practically, when troubleshooting, combine these queries: find the package with rpm -qf, then run rpm -qi for details and rpm -ql for file locations. These commands provide the deterministic answers you need when editing config files or verifying that an install placed files where expected.

content.html:
Commands
rpm -qa
rpm -qa | grep httpd
rpm -qi httpd
rpm -ql tree
rpm -qf /usr/bin/tree
Use these commands to find packages, inspect versions and vendor info, and locate installed files for editing or removal.
Example workflow
  1. Find package owning a file: rpm -qf /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf
  2. Inspect package metadata: rpm -qi httpd
  3. List all installed files: rpm -ql httpd
Pro tip: Pipe rpm -qa into grep to quickly locate a package by partial name when the list is long.

screens.title: Verifying packages with rpm -V
screens.narratorSegment: Package verification is a powerful auditing feature of rpm. When you run rpm -V package_name, rpm compares each installed file against attributes stored in the RPM database. It checks file size, MD5 checksum, permissions, file type, owner, group, and modification time. The command prints a line for each file that differs, prefixed with a set of flags indicating the specific differences. For example, a 'T' indicates modification time change, while an 'S' reports size change, and an '5' indicates checksum differences. A practical use case is auditing configuration files: if an administrator suspects unauthorized edits to /etc/httpd/conf/httpd. conf, rpm -V httpd will flag that change. A common misconception is that rpm -V can repair files; it cannot — it only reports discrepancies so you can take corrective action. In a lab, you can simulate a change by touching or editing a file that belongs to a package and then re-running rpm -V to see the flags. Interpreting those flags helps you decide whether to restore a file from backup, reinstall the package, or accept the intentional change. Verification is a vital tool when you need to detect and reason about filesystem-level modifications.

keyIdea.title: Verification

content.html:
Verify
Use rpm -V to audit files
Command and example flags you might see:
rpm -V httpd
# Output example flags explained
# S file size changed
# 5 checksum mismatch
# T mtime changed
# M mode (permissions) changed
Practical steps
  1. Run rpm -V package_name to get verification output.
  2. Interpret flag letters to determine what changed.
  3. Decide: restore from backup, reinstall the package, or accept the change.
Simulation: touch a binary or edit a config and re-run rpm -V to observe the change flags during a safe lab exercise.

screens.title: Removing packages with rpm -e
screens.narratorSegment: Removing a package with rpm uses the -e (erase) option: sudo rpm -e package_name. rpm will check the RPM database to ensure no other installed package requires the target package; if dependencies exist, rpm will refuse to remove the package and report the dependent packages. This behavior protects the system from accidentally breaking other software. If you truly intend to remove a package and its dependents, use dnf remove which can remove dependent packages as well after warning you of the impact. A common misconception is that rpm -e deletes all files of the package unconditionally; rpm removes files known in its database but will not remove files if their ownership has changed or files were altered in ways rpm cannot safely reverse. Before removing a package, use rpm -q --whatrequires package_name to see what depends on it. Also use rpm -ql package_name to note configuration files that might need saving. In emergency scenarios where dependency trees are complex, carefully evaluate the impact or work in a staging environment. Proper use of rpm -e, with pre-checks, keeps systems stable and prevents accidental breakages.

If you truly intend to remove a package and its dependents, use dnf remove which can remove dependent packages as well after warning you of the impact. A common misconception is that rpm -e deletes all files of the package unconditionally; rpm removes files known in its database but will not remove files if their ownership has changed or files were altered in ways rpm cannot safely reverse. Before removing a package, use rpm -q --whatrequires package_name to see what depends on it. Also use rpm -ql package_name to note configuration files that might need saving. keyIdea.title: Safe removal
keyIdea.text: rpm -e removes a package but blocks if other installed packages depend on it; inspect reverse dependencies before erasing.

content.html:
Erase
Removing a package
sudo rpm -e tree
rpm -q --whatrequires tree
rpm -ql tree
Check reverse dependencies and file lists before erasing to avoid breaking other packages or losing configs you need to back up.
Scenario
If rpm -e refuses due to dependencies, consider dnf remove which will present a dependency plan. Never forcibly remove packages without understanding the consequences on production systems.
Warning: Removing shared libraries can render other packages unusable; always inspect what requires the package first.

screens.title: Dependency Hell — how rpm and DNF differ
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency problems occur when packages require other packages that are not present or have conflicting requirements. With rpm, missing dependencies are immediately visible because rpm does not resolve them for you. When you try to install a. rpm that depends on a library, rpm will fail and list the missing dependencies. This makes rpm useful for revealing exact missing requirements, but it also leaves you to obtain those RPMs manually. DNF reduces the risk of dependency hell by consulting repositories and installing required packages automatically. However, automatic resolution can sometimes hide complex conflicts or upgrade choices, which is why understanding the low-level requirements matters. screens.title: Hands-on lab walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This guided lab shows the exact sequence you'd perform to practice rpm safely in a disposable environment. First, obtain or prepare a local RPM; if you have repository access, run dnf download tree --destdir=/tmp to fetch the RPM to /tmp, or place an existing tree-1.8.0-1. el8. x86_64. rpm there. Next, attempt the install with sudo rpm -ivh /tmp/tree-1.8.0-1. el8. x86_64. rpm and watch for dependency errors. This stepwise routine gives you a reproducible way to learn install, query, verification, and erase operations.

Lab objectives
Download or stage a local RPM, install with rpm, inspect files, verify package integrity, simulate a change, and clean up by removing the package.
Step-by-step terminal commands

# dnf download tree --destdir=/tmp

# Install locally

Verification and cleanup

screens.title: Troubleshooting with rpm when DNF fails
screens.narratorSegment: When DNF fails or repositories are unavailable, rpm becomes the diagnostic and recovery tool. If a DNF transaction fails partway, the low-level rpm queries reveal the exact package state. For example, use rpm -qa and rpm -qi to confirm which version is recorded in the RPM database. Use rpm -ql to find files that may be missing or misplaced. If a package shows as installed but files are corrupted or altered, rpm -V will reveal which files differ and the nature of the change, guiding whether to reinstall the package or restore files. In cases of broken dependencies reported by DNF, run rpm -e carefully to remove problematic packages only after checking what requires them via rpm -q --whatrequires. For more complex recovery, you may need to install specific RPMs manually in an order that satisfies dependencies. A common pitfall is making forced changes without documenting them; always keep notes or backups so you can roll back. Using rpm for diagnosis gives you clear, low-level evidence about package metadata and file attributes that helps you make safe recovery decisions when higher-level tools cannot complete their work.

Diagnostic commands

rpm -qi package_name
rpm -ql package_name
rpm -V package_name

These commands provide the evidence you need to decide whether to reinstall, restore, or remove packages safely.

In this lesson we focus on RPM, the low-level package format and utility beneath DNF on RHEL systems. You will learn why RPM matters: it is the single-file package format every higher-level tool uses, and it gives you direct control when you must install a file locally, inspect a package’s file list, verify integrity, or troubleshoot repository problems. We’ll show the standard commands you'll use — install, upgrade, query, verify, and erase — and explain the differences between RPM and DNF. For example, RPM installs a single file but does not automatically resolve dependencies, whereas DNF manages collections and resolves relationships from repositories. Throughout the lesson you’ll practice installing a local RPM, listing its installed files, verifying those files against the RPM database, and safely removing the package. Understanding RPM helps when you have no network, when you must audit changes, or when DNF hides a low-level failure. By the end, you’ll know when to use rpm directly and how to read its output to diagnose problems. What scenario might push you to use rpm instead of DNF on a production host?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to use RPM as a focused, low-level package tool on RHEL systems. First, you'll understand RPM's role underneath DNF: it defines the. rpm file format and manages an on-disk database of package metadata. Second, you'll be able to install and upgrade packages directly from local. rpm files using the correct rpm options, and you will understand when those commands might fail due to missing dependencies. Third, you'll learn to query the RPM database to list installed packages and the files a package owns, and to inspect package metadata such as version and vendor. Finally, you will perform package verification and removal: use rpm -V to detect file changes and rpm -e to safely erase a package while recognizing dependency errors. These objectives give you precise control for offline installs, audits, and targeted troubleshooting when higher-level tools are insufficient.

These practical objectives focus on commands and observable outcomes so you can practice safely. You will install a package from a local file and observe dependency errors when prerequisites are missing. You will query the RPM database to find where configuration files and binaries were placed, which helps when you must edit or audit them. You will run rpm -V to detect modified files and learn how to interpret the verification flags it prints. Finally, you will remove a package with rpm -e and understand the dependency checks that will block removal if other packages rely on it. Practicing these tasks in a disposable environment or container is recommended so you can safely simulate a file change and see rpm -V report it. These hands-on skills prepare you for offline installs, quick audits, and targeted troubleshooting when DNF cannot be used.

Start by clarifying a common confusion: DNF and RPM are not competing package formats; they occupy different levels of the toolchain. RPM defines the package format and provides commands to operate on single. rpm files and the local RPM database. DNF is a higher-level package manager that uses repositories and resolves dependencies for you. Use rpm when you need precise, local control: installing a single downloaded file, querying exactly which files belong to a package, or verifying file integrity against the RPM database. Use DNF for day-to-day updates, installs from repositories, and when dependency resolution is essential. A useful mental model is that DNF manages collections and relationships, while rpm manages individual package artifacts. Common misconception: rpm will not magically fetch dependencies. If you try to install a. rpm that requires other packages, rpm will fail and report missing dependencies. Conversely, DNF will consult configured repositories and try to install required packages automatically. In practice, system administrators often use rpm for offline installs, forensic verification, or surgical fixes when DNF's higher-level behavior is not desired. As you practice, reflect on a scenario where a local vendor supplies a single. rpm for a custom tool — which tool do you pick and why?

The RPM database is the local record the rpm utility uses to track installed packages, their metadata, and the files they installed. On RHEL systems this database is typically stored under /var/lib/rpm. It contains details such as package name, version, release, installed file list, ownership, permissions, and checksums that rpm -V uses for verification. Think of the database as the authoritative ledger that lets you ask: which package owns /usr/bin/tree? Or what version of httpd is installed? When you run rpm -qa you query that ledger to list installed packages. When you run rpm -ql package_name you ask which files that package deposited. Importantly, the database is how rpm can detect unauthorized changes: rpm -V compares the current file state against the stored metadata. A common misconception is that the database contains copies of files; it does not — it contains metadata and hashes. If the database becomes corrupted, rpm commands will fail to report accurate package state, so backups or careful recovery procedures are necessary on production servers. Understanding what the database holds helps you interpret query outputs and verification flags during audits and troubleshooting.

Installing a local. rpm file with rpm -ivh is a direct, single-file operation. The -i flag requests an install, -v enables verbose output so you see progress, and -h prints hash marks as a simple progress indicator. When you run sudo rpm -ivh /path/to/package. rpm, rpm unpacks the package scripts and files, records metadata in the RPM database, and places the files on disk. However, rpm does not fetch or install missing dependencies; if the package requires libraries or other packages that are not present, rpm will stop and report missing dependencies. That output is your clue: it tells you exactly which packages are required. To resolve those dependencies you can either install the missing RPMs manually, use dnf to fetch them, or use dnf download to obtain RPM files for offline installation. A typical misconception is that adding -U is necessary for installing any new version; -ivh is specifically an install, while -Uvh can both install and upgrade. When a package conflicts with an existing one, rpm will return an error explaining the conflict. In practice, test local installs inside a container or VM so you can safely see dependency failures and learn how to retrieve and satisfy prerequisites.

Upgrading a package with rpm uses the -U flag: rpm -Uvh /path/to/package. rpm. This command installs the new package and removes the old one in the same operation if an earlier version exists. If no prior version is present, -Uvh will simply install the package. The verbose and hash options behave the same as with install. Important: rpm will not automatically resolve any new dependencies introduced by the upgraded version; if the upgrade requires additional packages that are missing, rpm will fail and report the missing items. For routine system updates and dependency-aware upgrades, prefer dnf update because it will consult repositories and try to satisfy requirements automatically. However, rpm -Uvh is useful when you must apply a vendor-supplied update from an offline medium or when you want deterministic control over the exact RPM file being installed. A misconception to avoid is that -Uvh will prevent conflicts: if the new package conflicts with others or introduces incompatible changes, rpm will fail and provide an error. As a best practice, test upgrades in a staging environment or use dnf when networked repositories can provide resolving assistance.

Querying the RPM database is the heart of understanding what is installed and where its files reside. The simplest command is rpm -qa, which lists all installed RPM packages by name. Because the output can be long, you often pipe it to grep to find a package of interest, for example rpm -qa | grep httpd. To see package metadata such as version, vendor, build date, and description, use rpm -qi package_name. To list all files installed by a package, use rpm -ql package_name. This last command helps when you need to locate configuration files or binaries a package provides. Another useful query is rpm -qf /path/to/file which tells you which package owns a specific file on disk. A common mistake is confusing package names used by rpm with the filenames of RPM archives; rpm commands use package names for queries (not the. rpm filename). Practically, when troubleshooting, combine these queries: find the package with rpm -qf, then run rpm -qi for details and rpm -ql for file locations. These commands provide the deterministic answers you need when editing config files or verifying that an install placed files where expected.

Package verification is a powerful auditing feature of rpm. When you run rpm -V package_name, rpm compares each installed file against attributes stored in the RPM database. It checks file size, MD5 checksum, permissions, file type, owner, group, and modification time. The command prints a line for each file that differs, prefixed with a set of flags indicating the specific differences. For example, a 'T' indicates modification time change, while an 'S' reports size change, and an '5' indicates checksum differences. A practical use case is auditing configuration files: if an administrator suspects unauthorized edits to /etc/httpd/conf/httpd. conf, rpm -V httpd will flag that change. A common misconception is that rpm -V can repair files; it cannot — it only reports discrepancies so you can take corrective action. In a lab, you can simulate a change by touching or editing a file that belongs to a package and then re-running rpm -V to see the flags. Interpreting those flags helps you decide whether to restore a file from backup, reinstall the package, or accept the intentional change. Verification is a vital tool when you need to detect and reason about filesystem-level modifications.

Removing a package with rpm uses the -e (erase) option: sudo rpm -e package_name. rpm will check the RPM database to ensure no other installed package requires the target package; if dependencies exist, rpm will refuse to remove the package and report the dependent packages. This behavior protects the system from accidentally breaking other software. If you truly intend to remove a package and its dependents, use dnf remove which can remove dependent packages as well after warning you of the impact. A common misconception is that rpm -e deletes all files of the package unconditionally; rpm removes files known in its database but will not remove files if their ownership has changed or files were altered in ways rpm cannot safely reverse. Before removing a package, use rpm -q --whatrequires package_name to see what depends on it. Also use rpm -ql package_name to note configuration files that might need saving. In emergency scenarios where dependency trees are complex, carefully evaluate the impact or work in a staging environment. Proper use of rpm -e, with pre-checks, keeps systems stable and prevents accidental breakages.

This makes rpm useful for revealing exact missing requirements, but it also leaves you to obtain those RPMs manually.
